construction_notes: HRQoL: EQ-5D-5L descriptive system (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression; five severity levels each) scored with the Danish value set, anchored at 0 for death and 1 for perfect health (Table 1, p. 89).
SWB: single life-satisfaction item on an 11-point 0-10 end-defined scale, rescaled to 0-100 (Table 1, p. 89).
Health care utilisation: all types of GP services, normal office hours only (Monday to Friday, 8AM to 16PM), measured weekly, only weeks following survey completion (weeks 17-52) (Table 1, p. 89).
Previous health care utilisation: average number of GP services over the three previous years, 2016-2018 (2017-2019 for the 2020 robustness check) (Table 1, p. 89).

Sample descriptives (Appendix Table A2, reported on p. 89): 47.3% men, average age 64.5 years, 4.6% non-ethnic Danish background, 23.2% live alone, 1.8 children on average, 14.1 average years of education, average family income DKK 337,426, mean Charlson Comorbidity Index 0.43.

Outcome and regressor distributions (p. 90): GP services range 0 (13.8% of individuals) to 169, mean 8.69 (SD = 9.51); HRQoL mean 0.88, range -0.63 to 1 (SD = 0.18); SWB range 0 to 100, mean 82.0 (SD = 17.06); correlation between HRQoL and SWB 0.49.
All Table 2 regressions use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and N = 6,484; covariates other than HRQoL and SWB are measured in 2019.

claims.statement: Controlling only for HRQoL, a higher SWB score is associated with a higher number of services provided in general practice in weeks 17-52 of 2019.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional independence / no unobserved confounding: conditional on the covariates entered in this column (HRQoL), the regressor is as good as randomly assigned with respect to the number of GP services, so the partial regression coefficient recovers the relationship of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state that they add sociodemographic covariates because they 'may act as confounders' and that they 'seek to overcome' confounding by including them; they also concede that confounding may remain. No balance test or formal ignorability claim is made.

key_assumptions.assumption: No reverse causality: health care utilisation does not cause SWB, i.e. the arrow runs from SWB to GP utilisation and not the other way round.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Columns (5) and (6) control for health care utilisation predating the SWB measurement (average GP services 2016-2018) and yield similar results; the authors read this as evidence that it is SWB that affects utilisation and not vice versa, while conceding that this likely overcontrols.

estimand.formal_query: E[number of GP services in weeks 17-52 of 2019 | regressor = r+1, covariates] - E[number of GP services | regressor = r, covariates]; a covariate-adjusted association, not a do()-contrast

population.description: Danish citizens aged 50-80 who responded to a representative cross-sectional web survey administered by Statistics Denmark in spring 2019 and were linkable to administrative registers for 2016-2020
population.period: survey spring 2019 (weeks 12-16); outcome weeks 17-52 of 2019; register data 2016-2020
subgroups_defined: levels of HRQoL (Fig. 1 plots HRQoL = 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95 and 1)
population.selection: 15,072 individuals invited; 6,807 (45%) returned a fully completed questionnaire; 323 further excluded for missing information, death or emigration during 2016-2020; 6,484 remain

identification.source_of_variation: No design-based variation: cross-sectional between-person variation in self-reported SWB and HRQoL among 2019 survey respondents, adjusted by regression for observed sociodemographics and (columns 5-6) for GP utilisation predating the survey. The authors call the study exploratory.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional independence / no unobserved confounding: conditional on the covariates entered in this column (HRQoL), the regressor is as good as randomly assigned with respect to the number of GP services, so the partial regression coefficient recovers the relationship of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state that they add sociodemographic covariates because they 'may act as confounders' and that they 'seek to overcome' confounding by including them; they also concede that confounding may remain. No balance test or formal ignorability claim is made.

key_assumptions.assumption: No reverse causality: health care utilisation does not cause SWB, i.e. the arrow runs from SWB to GP utilisation and not the other way round.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Columns (5) and (6) control for health care utilisation predating the SWB measurement (average GP services 2016-2018) and yield similar results; the authors read this as evidence that it is SWB that affects utilisation and not vice versa, while conceding that this likely overcontrols.

key_assumptions.assumption: No remaining latent common cause of SWB and health care utilisation. The authors concede this may fail: SWB might be confounded by other structural barriers, e.g. employment or caregiving demands, or transportation needs, and might itself mediate personality traits.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the authors argue only that such mechanisms 'do not undermine' the finding that SWB is an independent predictor.

key_assumptions.assumption: SWB measured once, in the spring-2019 survey, is a valid stand-in for the SWB that governs care-seeking over weeks 17-52 of 2019; the cross-sectional design means the causal pathways cannot be uniquely identified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; stated as a limitation.

key_assumptions.assumption: Only the net of two opposing behavioural mechanisms is estimated: SWB as a need indicator (negative) and SWB as a barrier to investing in health (positive). A measured sign shows which mechanism dominates, not the size of either.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; stated as an interpretive limitation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection bias from survey non-response: the 6,484 respondents are informative about the relationship in the invited population. The authors explicitly say they cannot exclude that this fails, respondents having higher HRQoL, higher SWB and a greater propensity to seek care.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; the authors argue the resulting bias would attenuate rather than overturn the link ('albeit it may be underestimated') and report weighted regressions as a robustness check (Appendix Table A3).

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form: the conditional mean of the number of GP services is linear and additive in the regressors apart from the single HRQoL x SWB product term, with homogeneous slopes across individuals. No equation is printed and the restriction is neither stated nor tested.

heterogeneity.finding: The association between SWB and GP services differs across levels of HRQoL: the positive association is strongest at low HRQoL, and for individuals with perfect HRQoL a higher SWB tends to be associated with lower utilisation (Table 2 columns (2), (4), (6); Fig. 1).

ambiguities: The paper prints no coefficient, standard error or significance test for the SWB slope at HRQoL = 1; -0.0043 is the linear combination of the two printed coefficients of Table 2 column (2) and the significance is left null because the paper tests none. Fig. 1's HRQoL = 1 line falls from about 6.8 to about 6.3 services across the 0-100 SWB range with a 95% band that includes a flat line.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 1 Predicted change in health care utilisation as a function of SWB and HRQoL. Note: The figure displays predicted values of health care utilisation as a function of SWB and HRQoL along with their 95% confidence intervals (robust). We do not control for other covariates in the model (corresponding to column (2) in Table 2)

evidence.how: Marginal association of SWB with GP services at HRQoL = 1, computed from Table 2 column (2) as the SWB coefficient plus the HRQoL x SWB coefficient evaluated at HRQoL = 1: 0.1668 + (-0.1711 x 1) = -0.0043 GP services per SWB point. The paper prints neither this number nor a standard error for it; it states the sign in the Discussion (p. 90) and plots the corresponding HRQoL = 1 line in Fig. 1 (p. 91), which slopes gently downward with a wide 95% band.
